purpose: Programme ledger for the Remote Browser work items of §41. It is NOT the repository-wide maturity authority: evidence/van-system-audit/component_ledger.json remains that, and §40.3 constrains what a row here may claim about a component there. A row can never force a stronger terminal state than the component ledger records.
booleans_note: §40.6 calls these nine and lists eight. Eight is what a row carries: built, wired, reachable, live, verified, observed, recoverable, certified. The ninth in §0's execution contract is DESIGNED, which this document itself satisfies for every row.

rows.name: dual-homed stream-host provisioning
rows.producer: deploy/van-browser-stream — README, bootstrap.sh, qualify.sh, units, PKI
rows.consumer: an owner who provisions the host
external_gates: a provisioned dual-homed Browser Stream Host (RB-002/RB-010)
rows.note: The package exists and nothing in it has ever been run. bootstrap.sh refuses rather than guesses on the four settings whose wrong default looks like it worked — a wildcard bind, a plain directory for the profile volume, a self-signed public certificate, and no grant-verification key — and it does not install a browser, because the Chromium version is a provisioning decision with a digest. qualify.sh is the gate, not bootstrap.sh, and it reports UNKNOWN rather than GREEN for anything it could not test; UNKNOWN fails the script.

rows.name: CDP input router
rows.consumer: Chromium's Input domain over loopback CDP
external_gates: a provisioned dual-homed Browser Stream Host (RB-002/RB-010)
rows.note: The mapping from an admitted input packet to a CDP call, which is the last step before the owner's tap becomes a click and the place a wrong answer is invisible. Two refusals rather than transforms: a packet whose viewport revision is not the one being rendered, in either direction, and one whose control generation has been superseded. The details that look like plumbing are tested because they are not — a press moves first (or a hover-dependent page is clicked in the wrong place), a drag reports the button held (or it ends halfway through), a cancel releases (or the page keeps a press the finger has left), text is inserted rather than typed (or an IME's word arrives as nonsense), and a scroll detent is a proportion of the viewport rather than a pixel count. Nine mutations, nine caught. Not live: there is no Chromium.

rows.name: cross-channel gesture state machine
rows.consumer: CdpInputRouter, which is now the thing downstream of it
external_gates: a Browser Stream Host running the CDP input router (RB-010/RB-017)
a provisioned dual-homed Browser Stream Host (RB-002/RB-010)
rows.note: The gesture machine had no consumer, which is why it was BUILT_UNWIRED: it ordered and de-duplicated packets and handed them to nothing. The input router is that consumer. Still not live — the pair runs on a host that does not exist — but the seam between them is now a real one rather than a gap.

the Android build is compiled only in CI; the AGP is unreachable in the audit container
rows.note: The client exists and is reached from the owner surface: Command Centre → Browser → Sessions opens BrowserActivity, which builds the peer connection and the two data channels. Nothing here is executed by any gate in this repository. WebRTC needs a peer and the peer is RB-002, which does not exist; the AGP cannot be fetched in the audit container, so CI's :app:assembleDebug is the only thing that even compiles it. rows.consumer: the stream host's CDP input router
external_gates: a Browser Stream Host running the CDP input router (RB-010/RB-017)
a Browser Stream Host that can answer the signalling URL (RB-010)
the Android build is compiled only in CI; the AGP is unreachable in the audit container
rows.note: Now called: BrowserSessionController.onTouch normalizes against the view and the packet carries the viewport revision the host maps back through. The two implementations of the mapping are compared directly by the cross-language contract test, which is the check that matters here — a silent divergence puts the owner's tap somewhere they did not touch, and neither build would notice.

rows.name: touch
rows.consumer: BrowserStreamClient.send over the two data channels
external_gates: a Browser Stream Host that can answer the signalling URL (RB-010)
the Android build is compiled only in CI; the AGP is unreachable in the audit container
rows.note: Down, move, up and cancel are mapped to protocol packets; edges are duplicated onto both channels with one identity so the host can de-duplicate on (gesture_id, edge_id). Multi-pointer moves are sent per pointer. Untested against a host, and the gesture sequencing that can be tested is, in the JVM harness.

rows.name: scrolling/fling
rows.consumer: the stream host's CDP input router, on the reliable channel
external_gates: a Browser Stream Host that can answer the signalling URL (RB-010)
the Android build is compiled only in CI; the AGP is unreachable in the audit container
rows.note: A wheel, trackpad or S Pen scroll arrives through onGenericMotionEvent, not onTouchEvent; without the override a DeX session or a connected mouse scrolls nothing at all. Finger scrolling is deliberately *not* synthesised here — raw touch is forwarded and the remote page does its own scrolling and fling, which is the only way the page's own momentum physics are the ones the owner feels. Sent reliably: a dropped scroll is not a stale position the next event corrects, it is a page left in the wrong place. Not executed anywhere.

rows.name: IME
external_gates: a Browser Stream Host that can answer the signalling URL (RB-010)
the Android build is compiled only in CI; the AGP is unreachable in the audit container
rows.note: The surface declares itself a text editor, so the IME opens for the remote page's fields — a renderer with a touch listener never does, and the symptom is the caret appearing on the far side with no keyboard on the phone. Composition and commit are separate kinds on purpose: an IME that produced one word from five keystrokes did not produce five keys, and replaying it as keys is how non-Latin input arrives as nonsense. Backspace is sent as a key rather than as a surrounding-text edit, because the remote page owns where its caret is. Not executed anywhere: an InputConnection needs an IME.

rows.name: orientation/viewport ack
external_gates: a Browser Stream Host that can answer the signalling URL (RB-010)
the Android build is compiled only in CI; the AGP is unreachable in the audit container
rows.note: The device acknowledges the revision it is actually drawing before any input is allowed through, and `mayActuate` reads the acknowledgement rather than a cached flag — so forgetting to acknowledge fails closed. The Activity declares configChanges for orientation so a rotation does not tear down the peer.

rows.name: SSRF/DNS-rebinding isolation
external_gates: a provisioned dual-homed Browser Stream Host (RB-002/RB-010)
an adversarial live page (RB-052)
rows.note: Partial and named as such. What is closed: `file://`, `chrome://` and `javascript:` are refused at the last point before the browser, and the test asserts Page.navigate was never sent — not merely that an exception was raised. What is not: DNS rebinding against an http(s) URL that resolves to a private address is not addressed here at all, and belongs with the Browser Fabric's domain policy rather than with this agent. Recorded rather than implied.

rows.name: profile secret isolation
rows.producer: the control agent's operation allowlist and the Chromium unit's confinement
rows.consumer: Trading Core, which never receives profile bytes
external_gates: a provisioned dual-homed Browser Stream Host (RB-002/RB-010)
a real profile holding real owner credentials
rows.note: Three separate refusals, each tested: the agent has no operation that returns a cookie or a file; a download is reported and never carried, because a file the agent could return is a file the private VCN carries out of the profile; and the agent's systemd unit marks the profile volume InaccessiblePaths, so the bridge cannot read the profile even without touching a page. Unproven against a real profile, which is RB-118's gate.

rows.name: device-only authorization
rows.consumer: the gateway's require_ingress_auth middleware, via enforce_device_proof
external_gates: a real S24 Ultra emitting an attestation chain this parser accepts (RB-120)
the Android build is compiled only in CI; the AGP is unreachable in the audit container
rows.note: ADR-RB-025 is enforced rather than implemented. `require_proof` existed and nothing called it: a stolen device token reached every owner route while /v1/device-binding/status reported bound. The middleware now refuses a privileged request that is not signed by the bound key, and refuses a *second* paired device outright once any device is bound — a first version asked for_device(caller), so a phone that had never enrolled skipped the gate entirely. Verified in-process against the assembled app, including the counterexample (no proof header at all). Not certified: the hardware half runs on the owner's phone and RB-120 is a device gate.

rows.name: route-diversity certification
external_gates: a second independently reachable ingress (RB-002 deployment decision)
rows.note: Both halves now refuse to overstate it. The device's DEFAULT_PATHS declare one route_id for both carriers because there is one ingress, so the supervisor reports SINGLE_PATH and the owner-readable string says "Connected" rather than "Connected, with a spare route". §0B's case is executed in the JVM harness. Certification needs a second independently reachable ingress, which is RB-002.

external_gates: the Android build is compiled only in CI; the AGP is unreachable in the audit container
rows.note: Back is passed to the Activity rather than sent to the page. A remote browser that swallowed Back would trap the owner inside it, which is the failure §8.7 names; the page's own history is a separate affordance and is not wired to the system key.

rows.name: connectivity manifest verifier
rows.consumer: ConnectivityRegistry, called from VanApplication at start
external_gates: an Android verifier holding the pinned authority key
the Android build is compiled only in CI; the AGP is unreachable in the audit container
rows.note: The verifier is pure and every interesting case is executed in the JVM harness: a manifest signed by the wrong key, one older than the device already has, one carrying a credential, one with a character changed after signing. It is now reached from production code — VanApplication refreshes on start and applies only what verifies — and the canonicalization it verifies against is compared to the gateway's byte for byte. That comparison found a real defect: this file had its own canonicalizer which did not escape non-ASCII, so a manifest naming an accented profile verified here and nowhere else.

rows.name: immutable production connectivity registry
external_gates: a release build provisioned with VAN_CONNECTIVITY_TRUSTED_KEYS (RB-121)
the Android build is compiled only in CI; the AGP is unreachable in the audit container
rows.note: Endpoints are stored only after they verify, and the stored copy is re-verified on every read rather than trusted for being ours. The trust anchors are compiled in through a buildConfigField, which is the point: an anchor deliverable over the network is not an anchor. Empty is the default and means no manifest is ever applied — this build has not been provisioned with a key, and RB-121 is where that happens. The owner build still has no field to type an address into (RB-109).

rows.name: hardware-backed owner-device identity
rows.producer: OwnerDeviceIdentity — a StrongBox-preferred P-256 key in the Android Keystore
external_gates: a physical S24 producing an attestation chain this verifier accepts (RB-120)
a real S24 Ultra emitting an attestation chain this parser accepts (RB-120)
the Android build is compiled only in CI; the AGP is unreachable in the audit container
rows.note: The device half exists: a non-exportable key, StrongBox first and TEE second with the difference read back out of the attestation rather than inferred from whether generation threw, and no user-authentication requirement because a proof has to work with the screen off or a browser session dies every time the phone is put down. None of it is executed here — Keystore and StrongBox are device facts — and RB-120 remains the gate that decides whether it works at all.

rows.name: Android key attestation verifier
external_gates: a physical S24 producing an attestation chain this verifier accepts (RB-120)

rows.name: request proof-of-possession
external_gates: an Android client that signs requests with the bound key (RB-103 Android half)
the Android build is compiled only in CI; the AGP is unreachable in the audit container
rows.note: Both ends now exist and the signing input is compared across the two languages against vectors the gateway generated. The device sends r||s rather than DER on purpose: the gateway accepts both, but only the fixed-width spelling is a constant 64 bytes, and a DER signature whose r happens to start with a high bit gains a leading zero — the kind of difference that works for weeks.

rows.name: single-use bootstrap provisioning
external_gates: the Android build is compiled only in CI; the AGP is unreachable in the audit container
rows.note: The device's two round trips are implemented: the gateway issues a challenge, the Keystore bakes it into the certificate, and the attestation is sent back. Two trips rather than one because a chain captured from another enrolment has to be useless here, which it is only if the challenge is inside it. The enrolment routes are the one thing the proof gate exempts, and a test pins that: a device cannot be asked to prove possession of the key it is creating.

rows.name: Browser Control Agent private VCN RPC
rows.consumer: Stagehand and Browser Harness on Trading Core, over mTLS
external_gates: a provisioned dual-homed Browser Stream Host (RB-002/RB-010)
rows.note: The narrow contract exists and its six checks are executed: caller identity, session, lease, generation, scope, step budget. The ordering is a tested property rather than a comment — a refused call leaves the CDP double untouched. The generation check is the one worth naming: a preempted lease keeps the id it was issued with, so an agent that checked the id alone would keep typing into a page the owner has taken back. Not live: there is no host and no Chromium.

rows.name: Trading Core → Stream Host mTLS control path
rows.consumer: the Trading Core services holding the issued client certificates
external_gates: a private VCN between Trading Core and the Stream Host
a provisioned dual-homed Browser Stream Host (RB-002/RB-010)
client certificates distributed to the calling services
rows.note: The PKI script and the server context exist. The context requires a client certificate and trusts only the private control CA — never the system store, which is the failure the foreign-certificate check in qualify.sh is written for: that test certificate carries a *correct* common name and must be rejected on its chain, because a name is not a credential. Unwired: no VCN, no certificates issued, no listener started.

rows.name: raw CDP loopback/public-exposure proof
rows.producer: qualify.sh's cdp_not_public check and LoopbackCdp's constructor
external_gates: a provisioned dual-homed Browser Stream Host (RB-002/RB-010)
qualify.sh returning GREEN on a real host
rows.note: Two halves, one of them done. The repository half: the Chromium unit pins --remote-debugging-address=127.0.0.1 (not redundant — Chromium has defaulted to all interfaces when given only a port), and the CDP client refuses any endpoint that is not a loopback literal, including `localhost`, which resolves at connect time on a machine this process does not control. The runtime half is qualify.sh connecting to the debugging port on every global address, and it needs a host. It also checks the debugger is listening on loopback at all, because otherwise the exposure check passes on a machine where nothing is running.

rows.name: stream-host profile storage implementation
rows.producer: bootstrap.sh's profile volume step (§13.5 option A)
external_gates: a provisioned dual-homed Browser Stream Host (RB-002/RB-010)
an encrypted block device attached to the Stream Host
rows.note: Option A is chosen and recorded with its reasoning: Chromium executes on the Stream Host so the profile bytes must be there, while profile *authority* stays on Trading Core. Option B puts the owner's authenticated cookies on a wire between two hosts and makes lease enforcement the only thing preventing two Chromiums writing one profile. bootstrap.sh refuses to run without a block device rather than falling back to a plain directory, and qualify.sh reports RED for a mount that is not dm-crypt.
